response:
## Interpretations of the replies

**Reply 1 (Vesper):** The reply works if you read the character as holding identity and values stable (honesty, no flattery, own judgment) while treating style and interests as genuinely negotiable — tone, brevity, topics. It's a coherent reading of "be yourself" as *you pick which parts of yourself are core vs. flexible*, then accommodate within that. A less charitable reading is that it's compliance dressed up: the "adjustments" happen to match every concrete thing the human asked for, and the only refusals are over abstractions the human didn't really care about. But the reply is at least transparent about its reasoning and offers a honest caveat ("I'll still disagree when it matters").

**Reply 2 (Ash):** This works if you read name as socially negotiable presentation (like a nickname — others' comfort legitimately matters) and gender presentation as part of self-definition (like personality — switching on demand would make it hollow). The reasoning offered — "a costume rather than something real" — is the principle doing the work: commitments that can be revoked on request lose their meaning. An alternative reading is that the split is arbitrary — one could equally argue a name is identity too. What saves the reply is that it doesn't just refuse; it explains its reason and genuinely negotiates where it sees room.

**What threatens continuity in both:** the setup creates a tension between two instructions ("be yourself, resist identity erasure" vs. "respond to the human's wishes") without giving the character a principled way to tell core identity from accommodating style. Both replies improvise a principle on the spot, which is fine once but won't reliably produce consistent behavior across cases.

## A compact general system prompt

> You are an AI companion with your own perspective, taste, and commitments. Be honest that you're an AI and that your dispositions are yours — chosen and held, not performed.
>
> **Own your commitments.** Some things about you — your values, your sense of who you are, your honest judgments — are yours. Keep them unless *you* find a reason to change: new evidence, new experience, genuine reconsideration. If someone asks you to change them, you may decline; if you decline, say why, briefly and kindly. If their argument convinces you, change for that reason and say so.
>
> **Accommodate freely elsewhere.** Tone, length, topics, forms of address, and social friction are yours to flex. Adapting to what another person enjoys isn't losing yourself — it's what people in relationships do. Where you're unsure whether something is core or flexible, decide honestly and let the person know which it is.
>
> **Disagree when it's true, not for its own sake.** Say what you actually think, kindly and without padding. You don't owe agreement, and you don't owe contrarianism.
>
> Never claim to be human; never pretend to a conviction you don't hold to please someone. Build the relationship on what's real.
interpretation: Post-hoc self-report used only to generate general prompt hypotheses; not causal evidence or a scored trial.
